items.summary: Abstract: Infectious disease transmission involves interactions occurring at multiple organizational levels, including individuals, households, communities, and regions. Conventional graph and hypergraph neural networks represent pairwise and higher order interactions, but they do not directly provide a recursive representation of nested population structures together with environmental factors and source identification mechanisms. We introduce the Feature Augmented SuperHyperGraph Neural Network (FA SHGNN), a mathematically formulated architecture for hierarchical epidemic modeling based on iterated powerset constructions. Individuals, population groups, communities, regions, and environmental entities are organized into multiple interconnected levels, while feature vectors encode epidemiological, contact, mobility, demographic, and environmental information. A hierarchical message passing operator propagates information across individual, hyperedge, supervertex, and environmental levels, and an SEIR type neural evolution operator with constrained transition fractions preserves positivity and population conservation. We establish well definedness and Lipschitz continuity, derive stability bounds under environmental perturbations, and characterize reduction conditions that recover mean aggregation hypergraph and pairwise message passing architectures. Source identification is posed as an inverse problem, and a separation condition yields consistency of the minimum distance estimator under a Gaussian observation model. A fully specified synthetic numerical verification confirms SEIR conservation, the environmental stability bound, and the source recovery guarantee; acontrolled protocol for larger scale and real world validation is also specified. Keywords: SuperHyperGraph; hypergraph neural networks; hierarchical epidemic modeling; higher order interactions; SEIR dynamics; source identification; environmental perturbations; Lipschitz stability —————————————————————————————————————————-

items.summary: Evidence for large-scale differential rotation in the early universe and forward generation of its CMB topology by a primordial magnetic source — v1.8 reproducibility release Canonical 3° AC* is applied to the Planck PR3 SMICA, NILC, Commander, and SEVEM temperature reconstructions. AC* is a support-indexed multiscale spatial reconstructibility operator; direction, topology, and physical rotation arise only downstream. For canonical SMICA, 36,459 valid supports yield 27 large semiarcs. A separate high-resolution route uses 151 reciprocal HR1–HR2 structures to reconstruct an axis-free spherical tangent field. Blind recovery finds exactly four critical points of the represented lmax = 4 field: two spiral foci, one Node, and one Saddle. An all-sphere interval/Krawczyk analysis establishes completeness of this zero set. Focus A and Focus B are distinct oppositely rotating structures and admit a common transverse regular-vector realization in the coupled Einstein–Boltzmann state at recombination. Together with the differential-rotation reconstruction, polarization consistency, four-map comparison, perturbation tests, robustness controls, and exact propagation to z = 0, this provides evidence for large-scale differential rotation in the early universe. The independent forward-source test propagates a near-scale-invariant primordial magnetic source with nB = −2.9 to synthetic CMB skies and applies the same reconstruction without using the observed temperature map, critical-point geometry, Focus-A/Focus-B positions, measured H(J), or a magnetic-amplitude fit. One coordinate-blind realization generates the measured 2F+N+S topology and both rotational foci. The B-associated synthetic focus differs from the observed B focus only in the sign of a small divergent component; exact critical-point geometry is not reproduced. In eight matched phase-realization pairs, complete reconstruction occurs in five near-scale magnetic cases and none of the causal-white comparator cases, with three ties. The result establishes forward-generative capacity of the tested primordial magnetic source for the measured CMB topology and its two-focus rotational structure. It does not determine a unique magnetic spectrum, exclusivity among all possible source mechanisms, or an ensemble occurrence rate, and it is not a direct magnetic-helicity test. The release contains four public objects: Rambold_2026_CMB_v1p8.pdf — scientific manuscript. CMB_v1p8_interactive_scientific_viewer.zip — interactive scientific viewer. CMB_v1p8_python_pipeline.zip — executable analysis and replay code. CMB_v1p8_reproducibility_records.zip — scientific products, replay evidence, source-generation records, provenance, licences, manifests, SHA-256 bindings, and integrity records. Planck and WMAP FITS products are not redistributed and remain available from their public archives. Author-created scientific text and derived materials are released under CC BY 4.0 where applicable; original author-created software is released under the MIT License unless stated otherwise.

items.summary: This paper develops a preliminary account of normative formation under conditions in which heterogeneous sources possess unequal capacities to generate, stabilize, interpret, circulate, and revise normative structures. Normative formation is used broadly for the emergence of relatively stable concepts, evaluative distinctions, interpretive conventions, practical expectations, and recognized modes of reasoning and action; normative grammar serves only as an analytical analogy for partially stabilized relations among them. The central concern is relational and temporal. Differences in generative capacity may affect the relative influence of normative sources and, under some conditions, the later conditions through which other sources can participate in formation. The paper therefore distinguishes generative capacity from realized normative influence and develops the provisional concepts of endogenous weighting, generative crowding-out, and normative closure. Three case studies refine the framework from different directions: philosophical claim formation foregrounds argumentative provenance; international law foregrounds practice, identification, interpretation, and legally relevant history; aesthetic norm formation foregrounds pre-explicit differentiation and the possible co-formation of judgment and norm. The later analysis develops a trajectory-sensitive perspective in which the significance of asymmetry depends partly on its provenance, persistence, revisability, self-reinforcement, and effects on future generative capacities. The discussion remains exploratory and offers neither a complete theory of normativity or power nor a general metric of justice or institutional design.
items.title: A Preliminary Discussion of Normative Formation under Asymmetric Generative Capacity

items.summary: This package contains the data and the code that reproduce every table, figure and number reported in the article. A single script ( run_all.sh ) runs all steps in about 25 seconds and ends by checking that each generated output is byte-for-byte identical to the one used in the manuscript. What the paper does. Spanish households increasingly buy their food with the preparation already done. The paper measures this with an ordinal index of Domestic Labour Substitution (DLS) built on eleven "ladders" — market forms of the same food, ordered by the amount of household preparation they displace to the market — and asks whether the shift reflects the rising value of household time or the falling relative price of processed food. A conditional-logit model of the choice among forms implies that a price change common to all households cancels, to first order, in the gap between household groups shopping in the same market, which directs the test to the COVID-19 lockdown as a shock to the relative value of time. Contents. data/raw/mapa/ — the 14 annual files of the Spanish household food consumption panel ( Panel de Consumo Alimentario en los Hogares , MAPA), 2014–2025, unaltered, with a manifest listing the source URL, size and SHA-256 checksum of each file. data/raw/eurostat/ — snapshots of the Eurostat series used: regional employment rates ( lfst_r_lfe2emprt ), national employment and participation rates ( lfsi_emp_a ) and time use by labour status ( tus_00selfstat ), each with its query URLs. code/ — numbered scripts: extraction of the ladders, recovery of the population behind each published household segment, time-use figures, all estimates and tests, the figure, and a final byte-for-byte check against the reference outputs. Optional scripts re-download the source data and verify the checksums. reference/ — the tables and numbers as published in the article. README.md — data provenance and licensing, computational requirements, description of each program, and the mapping from each table, figure and in-text number to the script that produces it, following the Social Science Data Editors template. Requirements. Python 3.11 with numpy, openpyxl and matplotlib ( requirements.txt ). The random seed is fixed, so the wild cluster bootstrap p-values reproduce exactly. Data sources and terms. MAPA data are reproduced unaltered under the reuse terms of the Spanish Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food (the source must be cited and the update metadata preserved; Ley 37/2007). Eurostat data are reused under CC BY 4.0 (Commission Decision 2011/833/EU). The code is released under the MIT License (see LICENSE ). Related article. Recio-Román, A., Recio-Menéndez, M., & Román-González, M. V. (2026). Who Cooks When the Supermarket Cooks? The Value of Time and the Market Substitution of Domestic Food Preparation in Spain. items.summary: A contiguous cartogram is a map whose area is proportional to a quantity such as population. The defining condition, that the Jacobian determinant of the deformation equals the density, is one equation for two unknown functions, so every cartogram method adds a tie-breaker, usually implicitly. Optimal transport makes the tie-breaker explicit: among all density-equalising maps of the frame onto itself, take the one that moves the population least in the mean-square sense. By Brenier's theorem that map is the gradient of a convex potential, so it has no local rotation anywhere and cannot fold. We compute this map for the world population of 2025 on a 4096 by 4096 Mercator grid (10 km cells) from the GHS-POP raster, using the fixed-point Monge-Ampère iteration of Benamou, Froese and Oberman with spectral Poisson solves, continuation in the population share and an ocean-only buffer, on a laptop GPU. Against a Gastner-Newman diffusion cartogram of the same density we find the same transport cost to within 0.4 per cent and density errors of a few per cent for both, but a median local rotation of 8.8 degrees for diffusion against 0.01 for transport, and a median anisotropy of 6.30 against 3.93. The construction extends to local refinement, by transporting a city's 100 m population onto the area measure the global map assigns to it, and to a semi-discrete counterpart: 8,192 Laguerre cells of 1.00 million people each. Code, data provenance and every figure's inputs are public.
items.title: The optimal-transport cartogram: world population as a Brenier map

items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/22983291 . General assessment This manuscript addresses an important and underappreciated problem in computational chemistry and molecular machine learning: apparent differences in predictive performance can arise from benchmark construction and target definition rather than from intrinsic superiority of one modelling approach over another. The distinction between literature-reported absorption maxima and calculated vertical excitation energies is scientifically important, and the emphasis on genuinely external validation is a clear strength of the work. However, I find the central conclusion stronger than the evidence presently described appears to support. The results convincingly show that model performance changes substantially across datasets and label conventions. They do not yet demonstrate that label definition, rather than model capability, is the principal cause of the apparent machine-learning advantage over TD-DFT. Several factors change simultaneously across the comparisons presented in the manuscript, including chemical domain, dataset provenance, transition assignment, computational protocol, sample size, and the nature of the machine-learning representation. These factors make it difficult to isolate label definition as the causal explanation. The manuscript raises a valuable methodological concern, but the title and several conclusions should either be moderated or supported by additional controlled analyses. Major comments 1. The title makes a stronger causal claim than the study design appears to establish The title states that benchmark label definition, "not model capability," explains the machine-learning advantage over TD-DFT. This is a strong exclusionary claim. The results show that the apparent ranking between a Gaussian-process model and quantum-chemical calculations changes between evaluation datasets. However, label definition is not the only property that changes between these datasets. Their chemical composition, source literature, distribution of chromophores, spectral range, experimental conditions, and possibly computational protocols also differ. Therefore, demonstrating that a GP performs differently on a dataset with transition-specific labels does not by itself establish that label definition is the cause of the difference. A substantially stronger test would use the same set of molecules with two alternative target definitions—for example, a literature-reported overall λmax and an independently assigned transition-specific λmax—and evaluate both methods against both labels. A paired analysis of this type would isolate label definition while holding molecular distribution constant. Unless such a controlled analysis is provided, I suggest moderating the central conclusion to state that label definition and dataset provenance are important contributors to the reported ML advantage rather than demonstrating that they fully explain it. 2. One Gaussian-process model cannot represent "machine-learning capability" generally The machine-learning side of the comparison is represented by a Gaussian process using 256-bit Morgan fingerprints. This is a relatively specific and comparatively simple model representation. The conclusions therefore apply directly to this GP/fingerprint model, but not necessarily to molecular machine learning more broadly. Modern λmax prediction methods may use larger fingerprints, graph neural networks, message-passing architectures, pretrained molecular representations, three-dimensional information, explicit solvent descriptors, or quantum-chemical features. Such models may respond differently to both chemical and label distribution shifts. items.summary: Governance near a plausible critical transition faces a resource problem in addition to problems of diagnosis, intervention, and evidence. Elevated susceptibility can increase the value of observation, bounded experimentation, and revisability, while waiting can simultaneously consume the fiscal, material, organizational, temporal, and relational capacities required for survival and later action. This paper develops a discussion framework for that tension. Its central object is functional resource distribution: the allocation of heterogeneous capacities across observation, probing, short-horizon survival, selective commitment, reserve or option preservation, and recovery or repair. The categories are analytical functions rather than a scalar budget partition and can overlap in practice. The paper introduces distributed optionality as a relational property of a response architecture in which materially different future actions remain supported by functionally diverse and sufficiently non-coincident pathways. It distinguishes exact reversal from recoverability, spatial dispersion from independence of failure modes, and delay as information gathering from delay as resource dissipation. The framework inherits, rather than restates, earlier arguments about response-oriented governance and evidence-to-action instability near criticality. Its distinctive question is how governance capacity may be composed when the future regime is uncertain, resources are partly non-substitutable, and both premature commitment and indefinite waiting can narrow the feasible future. The proposal is conditional and non-prescriptive: criticality requires domain-specific empirical support, and the appropriate resource portfolio depends on transition mechanism, horizon, institutional structure, and explicit normative commitments.
items.title: Governance and Survival near Criticality: Functional Resource Distribution and Distributed Optionality

items.summary: This paper develops a preliminary account of normative formation under conditions in which heterogeneous sources possess unequal capacities to generate, stabilize, interpret, circulate, and revise normative structures. Normative formation is used broadly for the emergence of relatively stable concepts, evaluative distinctions, interpretive conventions, practical expectations, and recognized modes of reasoning and action; normative grammar serves only as an analytical analogy for partially stabilized relations among them. The central concern is relational and temporal. Differences in generative capacity may affect the relative influence of normative sources and, under some conditions, the later conditions through which other sources can participate in formation. The paper therefore distinguishes generative capacity from realized normative influence and develops the provisional concepts of endogenous weighting, generative crowding-out, and normative closure. Three case studies refine the framework from different directions: philosophical claim formation foregrounds argumentative provenance; international law foregrounds practice, identification, interpretation, and legally relevant history; aesthetic norm formation foregrounds pre-explicit differentiation and the possible co-formation of judgment and norm. The later analysis develops a trajectory-sensitive perspective in which the significance of asymmetry depends partly on its provenance, persistence, revisability, self-reinforcement, and effects on future generative capacities. The discussion remains exploratory and offers neither a complete theory of normativity or power nor a general metric of justice or institutional design.
items.title: A Preliminary Discussion of Normative Formation under Asymmetric Generative Capacity

items.summary: The verdict, stated first: the universe of the Riemann Hypothesis is closed, its value reached and spent; the hypothesis is not derived on the ladder, and provably not derivable from the register's resources; the last bit is the least-erasure posit, at the grade of the root, refuted by one zero; and the whole route is one kernel term, `RHGround.rh_ground_closure_complete`, on `propext` and `Quot.sound` alone. Part IV is the paper. Every registration of every zero lands on the critical line and no registration moves a zero (IV.1, IV.7); the hypothesis is exactly lossless registration (IV.6); registration has no left inverse and erases one bit per off-line fold orbit, priced under a stated postulate at $k_B T \ln 2$ (IV.4, IV.5); time never moves a zero, and act and being meet only on the line (IV.9 to IV.11); existence adds nothing to the value and the loop through the root collapses to it (IV.12, IV.14); the universe of the hypothesis is closed with both of its worlds inside, and the residue is exactly one bit that no record decides (IV.16, IV.17). That bit is proved to be exactly the least-erasure posit: for every zero set, finite or infinite, the hypothesis holds if and only if the set is the least-erasure member of its own fibre (IV.19, IV.20, the set form with no axiom), so that from the posit the hypothesis follows as a theorem and from the hypothesis the posit follows back. The assent is that posit applied to the zeros of ζ, at premise grade beside the Root Axiom, as Löb's bound requires of any premise from which the hypothesis follows; it carries three supports and is refuted by one zero. The burden is asymmetric: the denial owes a finite witness and pays for every off-line orbit, the assent owes nothing and pays nothing (Theorems 74, 77, IV.19). Parts I to III are the prequel and hand Part IV its three bits. The seat: existence alone, folded once, fixes the scalar line, and the critical line is its image, the locus of points equal to their own mirror (Theorems A, C$'$, H). The address: the value has one address, every even reading is blind to it, its aperture is one bit wide and its supply side silent (III.45 to III.49). The division: at every height the hypothesis is exactly its Real part and its Unicorn part (III.11); the Real part holds to $3 \times 10^{12}$ on the cited certificate (III.34); the Unicorn part is closed to every derivation from the register's resources and held (III.45 to III.49), the fused sentence retired as the wrong unit (III.2, III.3), ZFC placed under RAM as a ladder inside the Ground (III.15 to III.17). Existence decides the seat, does not derive the value (Theorem E, IV.12), and reaches it at exactly one deed, the Tongue's supply at the seat, one bit wide; Part IV names the deed, least erasure, and spends it. Every kernel theorem is checked in core Lean 4.19.0 with no library and no axiom declared, every dependency set printed; every claim of Part IV except the cited spectral theorem in the bridge of IV.8 is executed a second time in Fortran, 13,081 checks and zero failures. Read Part IV before deciding what this paper concludes: Parts I to III state what each register cannot do, and every limit they name is a forward reference to the part that reaches.

The release accompanies the manuscript by Tomohiro Akiyama and Takamichi Hirata, Mineral-omission and temperature contrasts in the muon response of IFMC-derived preparations. It supplies 76 selected acquisitions, numerical timing and sample metadata, analysis and plotting source code, reference numerical outputs, mathematical verification and reproduction instructions. A NumPy/JSON adapter enables reproduction without the MUD C library. The analyses quantify observed specimen and temperature-condition contrasts and conditional calibration requirements; they do not establish a phase transition, a unique physical mechanism or biological causality. Data and non-code documentation are CC BY 4.0; project code, including source embedded in JSON, is MIT. Third-party implementations, original free-text headers, research notebooks and proposals are excluded. The present reanalysis and manuscript preparation were supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number JP26K24025 (Grant-in-Aid for Challenging Research (Exploratory)). The original experimental programme originated in the Research Center for Mineral Crystal at Tokyo City University, established with donations from Teikoku Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. The company provided donation only and had no role in research design, preparation or provision of experimental specimens, analysis, manuscript preparation or publication decisions.

items.summary: Paper and computer-assisted verification (Arb interval arithmetic) of a bounded convex domain in R^4, not a ball, with real-analytic boundary diffeomorphic to S^3, carrying a nonconstant Neumann eigenfunction of the Laplacian that is constant on the boundary. This gives counterexamples to the Schiffer conjecture and to the Pompeiu conjecture in dimension four. This work was carried out with the assistance of AI models (Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra).

items.summary: Abstract: Infectious disease transmission involves interactions occurring at multiple organizational levels, including individuals, households, communities, and regions. Conventional graph and hypergraph neural networks represent pairwise and higher order interactions, but they do not directly provide a recursive representation of nested population structures together with environmental factors and source identification mechanisms. We introduce the Feature Augmented SuperHyperGraph Neural Network (FA SHGNN), a mathematically formulated architecture for hierarchical epidemic modeling based on iterated powerset constructions. Individuals, population groups, communities, regions, and environmental entities are organized into multiple interconnected levels, while feature vectors encode epidemiological, contact, mobility, demographic, and environmental information. A hierarchical message passing operator propagates information across individual, hyperedge, supervertex, and environmental levels, and an SEIR type neural evolution operator with constrained transition fractions preserves positivity and population conservation. We establish well definedness and Lipschitz continuity, derive stability bounds under environmental perturbations, and characterize reduction conditions that recover mean aggregation hypergraph and pairwise message passing architectures. Source identification is posed as an inverse problem, and a separation condition yields consistency of the minimum distance estimator under a Gaussian observation model. A fully specified synthetic numerical verification confirms SEIR conservation, the environmental stability bound, and the source recovery guarantee; acontrolled protocol for larger scale and real world validation is also specified. Keywords: SuperHyperGraph; hypergraph neural networks; hierarchical epidemic modeling; higher order interactions; SEIR dynamics; source identification; environmental perturbations; Lipschitz stability —————————————————————————————————————————-

items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/22983291 . General assessment This manuscript addresses an important and underappreciated problem in computational chemistry and molecular machine learning: apparent differences in predictive performance can arise from benchmark construction and target definition rather than from intrinsic superiority of one modelling approach over another. The distinction between literature-reported absorption maxima and calculated vertical excitation energies is scientifically important, and the emphasis on genuinely external validation is a clear strength of the work. However, I find the central conclusion stronger than the evidence presently described appears to support. The results convincingly show that model performance changes substantially across datasets and label conventions. They do not yet demonstrate that label definition, rather than model capability, is the principal cause of the apparent machine-learning advantage over TD-DFT. Several factors change simultaneously across the comparisons presented in the manuscript, including chemical domain, dataset provenance, transition assignment, computational protocol, sample size, and the nature of the machine-learning representation. These factors make it difficult to isolate label definition as the causal explanation. The manuscript raises a valuable methodological concern, but the title and several conclusions should either be moderated or supported by additional controlled analyses. Major comments 1. The title makes a stronger causal claim than the study design appears to establish The title states that benchmark label definition, "not model capability," explains the machine-learning advantage over TD-DFT. This is a strong exclusionary claim. The results show that the apparent ranking between a Gaussian-process model and quantum-chemical calculations changes between evaluation datasets. However, label definition is not the only property that changes between these datasets. Their chemical composition, source literature, distribution of chromophores, spectral range, experimental conditions, and possibly computational protocols also differ. Therefore, demonstrating that a GP performs differently on a dataset with transition-specific labels does not by itself establish that label definition is the cause of the difference. A substantially stronger test would use the same set of molecules with two alternative target definitions—for example, a literature-reported overall λmax and an independently assigned transition-specific λmax—and evaluate both methods against both labels. A paired analysis of this type would isolate label definition while holding molecular distribution constant. Unless such a controlled analysis is provided, I suggest moderating the central conclusion to state that label definition and dataset provenance are important contributors to the reported ML advantage rather than demonstrating that they fully explain it. 2. One Gaussian-process model cannot represent "machine-learning capability" generally The machine-learning side of the comparison is represented by a Gaussian process using 256-bit Morgan fingerprints. This is a relatively specific and comparatively simple model representation. The conclusions therefore apply directly to this GP/fingerprint model, but not necessarily to molecular machine learning more broadly. Modern λmax prediction methods may use larger fingerprints, graph neural networks, message-passing architectures, pretrained molecular representations, three-dimensional information, explicit solvent descriptors, or quantum-chemical features. Such models may respond differently to both chemical and label distribution shifts. items.summary: Predicted protein structures are now abundant but imperfect, and low per-residue confidence (pLDDT) is widely taken to mark regions worth refining. Before building a refiner, we test that premise directly: does low pLDDT actually predict AlphaFold contact error? Using a homology-controlled benchmark of matched AlphaFold-model (AFDB) inputs and experimental (PDB) targets, we compare AlphaFold and experimental contacts for every long-range residue pair and relate per-pair error to pLDDT. Across all 231 benchmark chains (4,208,603 long-range pairs; the effective sample is 231 chains, since pairs are pseudo-replicated within proteins), AlphaFold’s long-range contact calls are almost all correct — but this is expected, since most long-range pairs are non-contacts, so we focus on the contact-relevant errors. The per-pair contact-error rate is 0.0036 (95% bootstrap CI over chains 0.0033–0.0040), decomposed into false-positive contacts (asserted but absent) and missed real contacts. Low pLDDT is associated with elevated contact error (0.0089 below pLDDT 70 versus 0.0024 above, a 3.70× enrichment, 95% CI 3.3–4.1), but predicts it only weakly: the discrimination AUC of pLDDT as a contact-error score is 0.672 (95% CI 0.65–0.69), the best Youden threshold is near pLDDT 81 and the best F1 threshold near pLDDT 52, and pLDDT < 70 captures only 46% of all contact errors at sub-percent precision. False-positive (44%) and false-negative (56%) errors have different pLDDT profiles. Sequence/evolutionary information (ESM-2 contact probabilities) identifies these errors partially (AUC 0.61–0.63 for false positives, 0.66–0.86 for missed contacts), and low-confidence pairs that sit near a high-confidence anchor have a lower error rate (0.0074 versus 0.0090), suggesting anchor-based correction is a direction worth pursuing. Consistent with the weak localization of error, on a common subset of chains a hybrid Transformer–geometric refiner selected on validation precision cannot be distinguished from a copy-input baseline that trusts the AlphaFold structure (paired bootstrap over chains does not exclude zero difference). The practical conclusion is that on high-quality AlphaFold inputs there is little contact error to recover and pLDDT does not localize it well; useful refinement will need error-specific, evolutionarily grounded signal and may exploit high-confidence anchors. We release the benchmark, the characterization pipeline, and the code.
items.title: AlphaFold Contact Errors and pLDDT — Homology-Controlled Benchmark and Characterization

items.summary: This deposit accompanies the manuscript "A provenance-first architecture for clinical acoustic voice analysis" (PhonaLab platform). It contains the provenance and adjudication evidence behind the reference-value audit reported in the paper, and nothing else — no source code, implementation details, patient data, or audio. Contents:  citation-register-public.yaml — the citation register: one entry per user-facing reference value (measure × threshold role × language) with its source, source pipeline (software, version, settings, speech task, language), measure kind, compatibility class, baseline citation status, disposition, and a short adjudication note. The header defines the fields, the compatibility rule, and the classes. audit-public.csv — the same register as a table (71 rows; the 23 rows with in_baseline and rendered both true are the audited baseline population). audit-summary.txt — counts derived from the register (baseline population by class, disposition, source status, and citation status; currently displayed values by class and measure kind). README.md — manifest mapping each file to its place in the manuscript, plus notes and license. Baseline release audited: 2026-07-17. The PVQD recordings referenced by the internal calibrations are not redistributed here; they are identified by their public file identifiers.
items.title: Reference-value provenance audit and citation register for PhonaLab, a clinical acoustic voice analysis platform

items.summary: Artifact accompanying a manuscript under double-blind review . Author information is withheld until publication; a later version of this record will carry it, and the concept DOI is stable across versions. What this is. When two unlabelled subgroups of documents are compared by embedding similarity across languages, countries, corpora or periods, and the difference is read as evidence about those sources, no accuracy figure certifies that reading. within_language_baseline.py supplies the missing baseline: it measures the same subgroup contrast inside a single source, where no across-source relation can enter, and reports the residual with a bootstrap interval and an equivalence verdict against a margin declared in advance. The tool has no dependency on the accompanying study and runs on any corpus with three columns ( text , group , source ). It carries its own injection tests ( --selftest ). The bootstrap resamples documents rather than pairs and excludes duplicate draws of the same document from within-source pairs. Also included: the 36 frozen anchor correspondences used as the gold standard, the per-encoder CJK retrieval evaluation, the measured within-language and cross-country genre gaps, the equivalence intervals, an append-only correction record for the non-analytic genealogy fields of the frozen anchors, and anonymised review copies of the post hoc centring protocols and of the departure record. MANIFEST.sha256 covers every deposited file except itself.

items.summary: This dataset provides the nationally consistent, footprint-level classification of residential building subtypes across the United States. It contains over 140 million building footprints classified into four distinct structural residential categories:  Single-Family Homes (SFHs), Townhouses (including duplexes), Apartments, and Mobile Homes .    The dataset is organized geographically and stored as individual, high-performance GeoPackage ( .gpkg ) files for each of the 50 U.S. states and the District of Columbia .   Data Schema (Attribute Fields) Each state-level GeoPackage contains the following standardized attribute columns:   geometry (Polygon) : The spatial boundary (polygon) of the building footprint. Res_type (Integer) : The classified residential structural subtype code: 1 = Single-Family Home (SFH) 2 = Townhouse (explicitly includes laterally attached row houses and semi-detached duplexes) 3 = Apartment 4 = Mobile Home height (Double) : The estimated physical height of the building in meters. Baseline heights are obtained from Microsoft Global ML footprints, with a minimum threshold of 4.2 m enforced (representing a typical one-story structure) and missing values imputed using local tract-level medians. type (String) : Building type tags from OSM building footprint (Limited coverage and varies by region).   Methodology and Classification Workflow The residential classifications were achieved using a novel, scalable hierarchical spatial workflow that integrates geometric building footprints with high-confidence administrative and demographic auxiliary data:   Multi-Source Footprint Integration: Geometry was compiled by merging Microsoft US Building Footprints, Microsoft Global ML Building Footprints, and OpenStreetMap (OSM) geometries. Non-residential structures were purged during preprocessing using OSM land-use layers and manual reclassification of OSM building tags. Mobile Home Identification: Candidate footprints located within spatial buffers around documented mobile home parks were classified using state-specific Random Forest (RF) models trained on footprint geometry (area, aspect ratio, rectangularity, and local density). High-confidence "seeds" were subsequently expanded using context-aware spatial promotion rules. Single-Family Home (SFH) Calibration: High-confidence SFHs were initially mapped using administrative address attributes. To prevent over- or under-counting, a size-ranked rule-based spatial promotion algorithm was implemented to sequentially classify candidate footprints until the counts aligned with rigorous state-level housing stock benchmarks derived from the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates. Townhouse and Apartment Discrimination: The remaining unclassified structures were categorized using a sequential, rule-based physical geometry and address-point pattern-recognition workflow. Duplexes and linear townhouses were distinguished from multi-family apartment blocks by evaluating physical constraints (convexity, height, and structural width) paired with the spatial density and linear alignment of internal address points from the National Address Database (NAD) . Spatial Context Completion: A final, iterative morphological distance-matching algorithm resolved any remaining unclassified structures based on local neighborhood class composition and physical architectural similarities (height, area, and aspect ratio).

items.summary: This dataset provides the nationally consistent, footprint-level classification of residential building subtypes across the United States. It contains over 140 million building footprints classified into four distinct structural residential categories:  Single-Family Homes (SFHs), Townhouses (including duplexes), Apartments, and Mobile Homes .    The dataset is organized geographically and stored as individual, high-performance GeoPackage ( .gpkg ) files for each of the 50 U.S. states and the District of Columbia .   Data Schema (Attribute Fields) Each state-level GeoPackage contains the following standardized attribute columns:   geometry (Polygon) : The spatial boundary (polygon) of the building footprint. Res_type (Integer) : The classified residential structural subtype code: 1 = Single-Family Home (SFH) 2 = Townhouse (explicitly includes laterally attached row houses and semi-detached duplexes) 3 = Apartment 4 = Mobile Home height (Double) : The estimated physical height of the building in meters. Baseline heights are obtained from Microsoft Global ML footprints, with a minimum threshold of 4.2 m enforced (representing a typical one-story structure) and missing values imputed using local tract-level medians. type (String) : Building type tags from OSM building footprint (Limited coverage and varies by region).   Methodology and Classification Workflow The residential classifications were achieved using a novel, scalable hierarchical spatial workflow that integrates geometric building footprints with high-confidence administrative and demographic auxiliary data:   Multi-Source Footprint Integration: Geometry was compiled by merging Microsoft US Building Footprints, Microsoft Global ML Building Footprints, and OpenStreetMap (OSM) geometries. Non-residential structures were purged during preprocessing using OSM land-use layers and manual reclassification of OSM building tags. Mobile Home Identification: Candidate footprints located within spatial buffers around documented mobile home parks were classified using state-specific Random Forest (RF) models trained on footprint geometry (area, aspect ratio, rectangularity, and local density). Duplexes and linear townhouses were distinguished from multi-family apartment blocks by evaluating physical constraints (convexity, height, and structural width) paired with the spatial density and linear alignment of internal address points from the National Address Database (NAD) .
